title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
statement:
`nestedList` is a list in which every item is either an integer or another list of the same kind, so lists can sit inside lists to any depth, and any inner list may be empty. Write a class `NestedIterator` that hands out all the integers of `nestedList` one by one, in the order you meet them reading the whole structure left to right as if the brackets were erased.

- `new NestedIterator(nestedList)` sets up the iterator.
- `next()` returns the next integer and moves past it.
- `hasNext()` returns `true` if some integer has not been returned yet, and `false` once all of them have.

The judge builds the iterator and then repeats: call `hasNext()`; if it is `true`, call `next()` and append the result to a list. When `hasNext()` returns `false`, that list must equal the flattened integers.

The items of `nestedList` (and of every inner list) are `NestedInteger` objects, which are provided:

- `isInteger()` is `true` when the object holds one integer and `false` when it holds a list.
- `getInteger()` returns that integer (`null` for a list).
- `getList()` returns the array of `NestedInteger` items it holds (`null` for an integer).

Each case is `[["NestedIterator"], [[nestedList]]]`, with `nestedList` written in JSON as numbers and arrays, and the answer is the flat list of integers. (The TypeScript starter types `nestedList` as `Array<_Node | null>` only because the signature format has no `NestedInteger` type; its items are `NestedInteger` objects.)
constraints: Every integer in nestedList is between -10^6 and 10^6
In this app, lists nest at most 8 levels deep inside nestedList
notes:
## Intuition

The simplest plan flattens everything into an array in the constructor and then reads it out, which does all the work up front and stores every integer twice. A lazier iterator walks the structure only as far as it needs to. Reading nested lists left to right is a depth-first walk, and a depth-first walk can be paused if we keep its call stack ourselves: for each list we are inside, remember the list and the position of the next item to look at.

## Approach

1. Keep two parallel stacks: `lists` (the lists currently open, outermost first) and `positions` (the next index to read in each). Start with `nestedList` at position `0`.
2. `hasNext()` moves the top of the stack forward until it rests on an integer:
   - If the top list is used up, pop it; its parent's position was already advanced.
   - If the item at the top position is an integer, stop and return `true`.
   - Otherwise it is a list: advance the parent's position past it and push the inner list at position `0`.
3. If the stacks run empty, no integers remain: return `false`.
4. `next()` calls `hasNext()` so the top rests on an integer, then returns it and advances that position.

## Example 1, step by step

`nestedList = [[1, 1], 2, [1, 1]]`. The stacks start as one frame `(nestedList, 0)`. The first `hasNext()` sees the list `[1, 1]`, moves the outer position to 1 and pushes `([1, 1], 0)`; now the top item is `1`, so it answers `true`, and `next()` returns `1`. The second `1` follows the same way. Then the inner list is used up, so `hasNext()` pops it, finds `2` at outer position 1 and `next()` returns it. The last list gives `1, 1`, both stacks empty out, and `hasNext()` returns `false`. Result: `[1, 1, 2, 1, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) amortized per call: every list is pushed and popped once and every item is examined a constant number of times, so the whole iteration is O(N + L) for N integers and L lists.
- Space: O(D) for the stacks, where D is the nesting depth.

## Pitfalls

- Empty inner lists such as `[[]]` contain no integers; `hasNext()` must look past them, not just check whether the stack is non-empty.
- `hasNext()` may be called several times in a row; it must not consume an integer.
- Advance the parent's position before pushing an inner list, or the same list is entered again after it is popped.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lists` | stack of the lists currently being read, innermost on top |
| `positions` | for each open list, the index of its next unread item |
| `depth` | index of the top frame in both stacks |
| `list`, `position` | the top list and where reading continues in it |
| `item` | the `NestedInteger` holding the integer `next()` returns |
